questions.statement: What is the main idea of the announcement?
questions.context: You hear a short library announcement before the lunch break at your school.

options.text: The library closes early today for repairs
options.feedback: Correct! The library closes early today for repairs captures the gist because the speaker repeats the closing time and the reason as the central message.

options.text: New novels arrived in the library this morning
options.feedback: The option about new novels arrived this morning is wrong because the message never mentions new arrivals and it turns an invented detail into the main point.

options.text: The lunch break will be longer than usual today
options.feedback: The option about the lunch break will be longer today is wrong because lunch is only when you hear the message, not what the message is about.

options.text: Every student must return all books immediately
options.feedback: The option about every student must return all books immediately is wrong because the announcement orders no general return, so it exaggerates a normal rule.

questions.explanation: Listening for gist means asking what the speaker wants you to know or do overall. Focus on the first sentence, repeated key words, and the final instruction, and ignore interesting but secondary details.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which note captures the specific information you must remember?
questions.context: You hear a voicemail from a dental clinic confirming your next visit.

options.text: Appointment on Thursday at half past four in room two
options.feedback: Correct! Appointment on Thursday at half past four in room two is right because those three facts are the exact day, time, and place a listener must write down.

options.text: The clinic is closed every Thursday in the afternoon
options.feedback: The option about the clinic is closed every Thursday is wrong because the voicemail confirms an open appointment, so closed contradicts the real message completely.

options.text: The dentist is called Thursday and works afternoons
options.feedback: The option about the dentist is called Thursday is wrong because Thursday is the day of the visit, not a person name, so it confuses a time word with a name.

options.text: Appointments are available every Thursday without booking
options.feedback: The option about appointments are available every Thursday without booking is wrong because the message is a single confirmed booking, not a general open door policy.

questions.explanation: Listening for specific information means filtering numbers, days, times, and places from the rest. Train yourself to write only those facts during the first listen and check them on the second listen.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states the main idea rather than a supporting detail?
questions.context: You hear a teacher starting a short talk about recycling in your city.

options.text: Our city must reduce plastic waste this year
options.feedback: Correct! Our city must reduce plastic waste this year states the overall claim because the other sentences only give examples, numbers, or meetings that support it.

options.text: Plastic bottles can take centuries to decompose
options.feedback: The option about plastic bottles can take centuries to decompose is wrong because that striking fact is only evidence that supports the call to reduce waste.

options.text: The school collected two hundred bottles last week
options.feedback: The option about the school collected two hundred bottles last week is wrong because that number is one local example, not the general message of the whole talk.

options.text: Volunteers meet at the central park on Saturdays
options.feedback: The option about volunteers meet at the central park on Saturdays is wrong because the meeting place is a practical detail for action, not the central idea itself.

questions.explanation: A main idea is a general claim the whole passage defends, while details are numbers, examples, or dates. Ask yourself which sentence the other sentences prove, and that one is the main idea.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What do you predict the speaker will discuss next?
questions.context: You hear the opening of a science podcast about exploring life on Mars.

options.text: Evidence of water and possible living conditions on Mars
options.feedback: Correct! Evidence of water and possible living conditions on Mars follows logically because the opening promises life on Mars, and water is the first related subtopic.

options.text: A recipe for a traditional potato omelette from Spain
options.feedback: The option about a recipe for a traditional potato omelette is wrong because cooking has no link to Mars exploration, so it ignores the prediction clue completely.

options.text: The history of classical piano music in Europe
options.feedback: The option about the history of classical piano music is wrong because music history does not continue a science opening about another planet in any natural way.

options.text: The rules for a school football tournament next month
options.feedback: The option about the rules for a school football tournament is wrong because sport rules belong to a different context and break the thematic continuity of the podcast.

questions.explanation: Predicting while listening means using the introduction, the title, and key nouns to guess the next subtopic. Good listeners activate related vocabulary before the speaker continues, which makes fast speech easier to follow.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How does the speaker feel about the test?
questions.context: You hear a student telling a friend how she felt after a fast listening test.

options.text: She found it fast but useful and wants more practice
options.feedback: Correct! She found it fast but useful and wants more practice fits because she mentions speed as a problem yet values the activity and asks for extra exercises.

options.text: She found it slow, easy, and completely boring
options.feedback: The option about she found it slow, easy, and boring is wrong because she clearly says the speech was too fast, which is the opposite of slow and easy.

options.text: She is angry at her friend for causing the noise
options.feedback: The option about she is angry at her friend is wrong because her tone is self critical and friendly, with no blame directed at the friend at all.

options.text: She prefers silent reading and hates all audio tasks
options.feedback: The option about she prefers silent reading and hates all audio tasks is wrong because she asks for more listening practice, which shows motivation rather than rejection.

questions.explanation: To infer attitude, listen to adjectives, tone words, and what the speaker plans to do next. Words like useful, difficult, or again reveal feelings even when the speaker never says happy or sad directly.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the speaker purpose in this part of the visit?
questions.context: You hear a museum guide speaking to a group of visiting students.

options.text: To give safety instructions before entering the gallery
options.feedback: Correct! To give safety instructions before entering the gallery is right because she talks about staying together, not touching glass, and following the signal.

options.text: To sell souvenirs at the museum shop exit
options.feedback: The option about to sell souvenirs at the shop is wrong because no prices, products, or shop location are mentioned in this section of the talk.

options.text: To explain the life of a famous painter in detail
options.feedback: The option about to explain the life of a famous painter is wrong because she names no artist and gives no dates, so it mistakes a later part for this one.

options.text: To tell a funny story about her own childhood
options.feedback: The option about to tell a funny story about her childhood is wrong because the tone is formal and directive, with no personal anecdote or humor included.

questions.explanation: Identifying purpose means asking why the speaker is talking now. Imperatives like stay, follow, and do not touch signal instructions, while dates and names signal information and adjectives signal persuasion.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which notes show the most effective listening strategy?
questions.context: You hear a short lecture about study habits and you must take notes.

options.text: Key words, arrows, and two short examples only
options.feedback: Correct! Key words, arrows, and two short examples only works because selective notes capture structure and links without trying to copy continuous speech word by word.

options.text: Every single word dictated by the lecturer
options.feedback: The option about every single word dictated is wrong because full dictation is impossible at natural speed and leaves no attention for understanding the message.

options.text: Random drawings unrelated to the lecture topic
options.feedback: The option about random drawings unrelated to the topic is wrong because drawings without labels record no ideas and cannot help you review the lecture later.

options.text: Only the date written at the top of the page
options.feedback: The option about only the date written at the top is wrong because a date alone stores no content, so it fails the basic purpose of listening notes.

questions.explanation: Effective listening notes use key words, symbols, and short forms arranged with arrows or numbers. You listen for structure first and add one brief example per point, instead of chasing every word.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct order of events as heard in the story.
questions.context: You hear a classmate retelling a short story played on classroom audio.

options.text: Boy misses the bus, walks to school, meets the coach, joins the race
options.feedback: Correct! Boy misses the bus, walks to school, meets the coach, joins the race follows the narrative chain because each step causes the next one in the audio.

options.text: Boy joins the race, meets the coach, walks to school, misses the bus
options.feedback: The option starting with boy joins the race is wrong because joining happens last as a result, so placing it first reverses the cause and effect of the story.

options.text: Boy walks to school, misses the bus, joins the race, meets the coach
options.feedback: The option with walks to school before misses the bus is wrong because he only walks after missing transport, so the order breaks the logical sequence.

options.text: Boy meets the coach, misses the bus, joins the race, walks to school
options.feedback: The option starting with boy meets the coach is wrong because the meeting happens at school after the walk, not before the missed bus at home.

questions.explanation: Sequencing while listening depends on time markers like first, then, after that, and finally. Track those signals rather than the order in which you remember images, and link each event to its cause.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What cause and effect relation does the reporter describe?
questions.context: You hear a radio report linking heavy rain to traffic problems in the city.

options.text: Heavy rain flooded tunnels, so several roads were closed
options.feedback: Correct! Heavy rain flooded tunnels, so several roads were closed matches the report because the speaker connects flooding directly to the closures announced.

options.text: Heavy rain cleaned streets, so traffic moved faster
options.feedback: The option about heavy rain cleaned streets so traffic moved faster is wrong because the report describes delays and closures, which is the opposite result.

options.text: Heavy rain was forecast, so drivers celebrated happily
options.feedback: The option about heavy rain was forecast so drivers celebrated is wrong because no celebration is mentioned and the tone reports problems, not joy.

options.text: Heavy rain stopped at noon, so tunnels were built
options.feedback: The option about heavy rain stopped so tunnels were built is wrong because building tunnels is a long project, not an instant effect of rain stopping at noon.

questions.explanation: Cause and effect in listening is signaled by so, because, therefore, and as a result. Identify which fact is the cause and which is the consequence, and reject options that reverse them or invent a positive outcome.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence from the discussion is an opinion, not a fact?
questions.context: You hear two students discussing a podcast about video games and health.

options.text: Listening to game reviews for hours is the best way to relax
options.feedback: Correct! Listening to game reviews for hours is the best way to relax is an opinion because best expresses a personal value judgment that cannot be verified by data.

options.text: The podcast episode lasted twenty five minutes in total
options.feedback: The option about the podcast lasted twenty five minutes is wrong as an opinion choice because duration is measurable and therefore it is a checkable fact.

options.text: The guest is a doctor from the city hospital
options.feedback: The option about the guest is a doctor from the city hospital is wrong as an opinion choice because identity and workplace can be confirmed, so it is factual.

options.text: The episode was published on Friday morning
options.feedback: The option about the episode was published on Friday morning is wrong as an opinion choice because the publication date is recorded objectively and verifiable.

questions.explanation: Facts can be checked with numbers, dates, or records, while opinions use value words like best, should, or beautiful. In listening tasks, underline verifiable data and treat evaluations as opinions.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the word however signal in the part you heard?
questions.context: You hear a debate speaker contrasting city life with country life for teenagers.

options.text: A contrast between an advantage and a disadvantage just mentioned
options.feedback: Correct! A contrast between an advantage and a disadvantage is right because however always introduces an opposite idea after a previous point has been presented.

options.text: A list of three similar advantages without any change
options.feedback: The option about a list of three similar advantages is wrong because listing uses also, moreover, or in addition, not a contrast marker like however.

options.text: The end of the speech with thanks to the audience
options.feedback: The option about the end of the speech with thanks is wrong because closings use markers like in conclusion or finally, not a mid argument contrast signal.

options.text: A new story with characters unrelated to the topic
options.feedback: The option about a new story with unrelated characters is wrong because however connects ideas within one argument and never starts a separate narrative.

questions.explanation: Discourse markers guide listening. Contrast markers like however, although, and on the other hand warn you that the next idea opposes the last one, while addition markers continue the same direction.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What can you infer overwhelming means from how the host describes the market?
questions.context: You hear a travel vlog where the host calls a market overwhelming and lively.

options.text: Full of noise, crowds, and activity that is hard to take in
options.feedback: Correct! Full of noise, crowds, and activity that is hard to take in fits because lively plus hard to follow points to too much input at once.

options.text: Silent, empty, and calm with almost no visitors
options.feedback: The option about silent, empty, and calm is wrong because silent is the opposite of lively, so it contradicts the descriptive clue given by the host.

options.text: Closed for holidays with locked doors and signs
options.feedback: The option about closed for holidays with locked doors is wrong because a closed place cannot be lively, so it ignores the positive energy described.

options.text: Small and tidy with only two quiet stalls
options.feedback: The option about small and tidy with only two stalls is wrong because two quiet stalls would not feel hard to take in or overwhelming for a visitor.

questions.explanation: Inferring unknown words while listening means using nearby adjectives, examples, and tone. Combine lively with the crowded market scene to guess too much to process, then confirm with the next sentence.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Where is the speaker and who are the listeners?
questions.context: You hear a loudspeaker message with flight numbers and gate changes in a large hall.

options.text: In an airport terminal speaking to waiting passengers
options.feedback: Correct! In an airport terminal speaking to waiting passengers fits because flight numbers and gate changes are only announced in that travel setting.

options.text: In a classroom speaking to language students
options.feedback: The option about in a classroom speaking to students is wrong because classrooms do not announce gates or flights, so it mistakes the setting completely.

options.text: In a kitchen speaking to restaurant cooks
options.feedback: The option about in a kitchen speaking to cooks is wrong because cooks receive orders and recipes, never boarding calls or gate change notices.

options.text: In a stadium speaking to football players
options.feedback: The option about in a stadium speaking to players is wrong because coaches give tactics there, not flight information for travelers.

questions.explanation: To identify context, listen for background clues and key nouns like flight, gate, platform, or table. Match those content words to a place, then check who would need that information.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the gist of the announcement?
questions.context: You hear a morning school announcement about an afternoon charity run.

options.text: A charity run starts at three behind the gym and needs volunteers
options.feedback: Correct! A charity run starts at three behind the gym and needs volunteers sums up the time, place, and request that the speaker repeats twice.

options.text: Morning lessons are cancelled because of heavy snow today
options.feedback: The option about morning lessons are cancelled because of snow is wrong because no cancellation or weather reason is announced in the message.

options.text: The school gym will become a new library next year
options.feedback: The option about the gym will become a new library is wrong because future building plans are never mentioned and confuse location with purpose.

options.text: Exam dates have been moved to the spring term
options.feedback: The option about exam dates have been moved is wrong because exams belong to a different announcement type and no dates are changed here.

questions.explanation: Gist questions ask for the overall announcement in one line. Combine who, what, when, and where from the stressed parts, and discard options that change the event or invent new consequences.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence expresses the same idea in different words?
questions.context: You hear a coach say that phones must stay in lockers during training sessions.

options.text: Players are not allowed to bring phones onto the training ground
options.feedback: Correct! Players are not allowed to bring phones onto the training ground paraphrases the ban correctly because must stay in lockers equals a prohibition on the field.

options.text: Players must buy new phones before the next training session
options.feedback: The option about players must buy new phones is wrong because buying is never mentioned and it changes a storage rule into a shopping order.

options.text: Coaches will lock the training ground during every match
options.feedback: The option about coaches will lock the training ground is wrong because locking the ground is different from storing phones in lockers inside.

options.text: Training sessions will be recorded on phones by coaches
options.feedback: The option about sessions will be recorded on phones is wrong because recording contradicts the ban and reverses the speaker original prohibition.

questions.explanation: Recognizing paraphrase is central to listening tests. Look for synonyms and changed grammar that keep the meaning, such as must stay in lockers matching are not allowed to bring onto the ground.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which key words should you catch to understand the warning?
questions.context: You hear a fast weather bulletin warning about a coastal storm tonight.

options.text: Storm, coast, tonight, avoid, harbor
options.feedback: Correct! Storm, coast, tonight, avoid, harbor are the content words that carry the warning because they name the danger, place, time, and action.

options.text: Beautiful, sunny, picnic, joyful, holiday
options.feedback: The option about beautiful, sunny, picnic, joyful, holiday is wrong because those pleasant words point to good weather and miss the urgent warning completely.

options.text: Recipe, sugar, oven, tasty, dinner
options.feedback: The option about recipe, sugar, oven, tasty, dinner is wrong because cooking vocabulary has no link to a storm bulletin and would mislead the listener.

options.text: Novel, chapter, author, page, library
options.feedback: The option about novel, chapter, author, page, library is wrong because reading words belong to a book context, not to an urgent coastal weather alert.

questions.explanation: In fast speech, stressed nouns, verbs, places, and time words carry meaning while grammar words blur. Train your ear to catch those content words first and reconstruct the message from them.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which example best supports the speaker claim?
questions.context: You hear a talk arguing that school gardens improve student health and focus.

options.text: Students who garden weekly eat more vegetables and concentrate better
options.feedback: Correct! Students who garden weekly eat more vegetables and concentrate better supports the claim because it links gardening directly to health and focus results.

options.text: The school garden has a green fence and ten wooden benches
options.feedback: The option about the garden has a green fence and benches is wrong because describing furniture proves nothing about health or concentration effects.

options.text: Gardens were first planted in ancient times by kings
options.feedback: The option about gardens were first planted in ancient times is wrong because history does not show current benefits for these particular students.

options.text: One teacher likes roses because they smell very sweet
options.feedback: The option about one teacher likes roses is wrong because personal taste in flowers is irrelevant to student health and cannot support the argument.

questions.explanation: A supporting example must connect the general claim to concrete results. Ask whether the example shows the claimed effect in action, and reject mere descriptions, history, or personal tastes.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What conclusion can you infer even though it is not stated directly?
questions.context: You hear a student podcast reviewing a new study app with mixed results.

options.text: The app helps with vocabulary but is weak for listening practice
options.feedback: Correct! The app helps with vocabulary but is weak for listening practice follows because she praises word games yet complains that audio tasks often freeze.

options.text: The app is perfect for every skill and has no problems at all
options.feedback: The option about the app is perfect for every skill is wrong because she reports frozen audio and limited dialogues, which contradicts a claim of perfection.

options.text: The app teaches cooking and fixes bicycles very quickly
options.feedback: The option about the app teaches cooking and fixes bicycles is wrong because those functions are never mentioned and lie outside a study app review.

options.text: The app was never tested by the speaker or her friends
options.feedback: The option about the app was never tested is wrong because she describes weeks of personal use with friends, so testing clearly happened.

questions.explanation: Inference in listening means joining praised points with complaints to reach an unstated judgment. List what worked and what failed, then choose the balanced conclusion that both sides support.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which response shows critical listening to this claim?
questions.context: You hear an online review claiming one energy drink makes you study all night.

options.text: Check other sources and ask for evidence before believing the promise
options.feedback: Correct! Check other sources and ask for evidence before believing the promise shows critical listening because it demands proof instead of accepting excitement as fact.

options.text: Buy ten cans at once because the speaker sounds excited
options.feedback: The option about buy ten cans at once is wrong because acting on excitement alone accepts advertising without questioning health effects or proof.

options.text: Share the link immediately with the whole class group
options.feedback: The option about share the link immediately is wrong because spreading an unverified promise can mislead others and skips the evaluation step entirely.

options.text: Ignore every review on the internet without thinking
options.feedback: The option about ignore every review without thinking is wrong because blanket rejection is not critical either, since it refuses to weigh any evidence at all.

questions.explanation: Critical listening asks who benefits, what evidence exists, and whether other sources agree. Excited tone and single stories are not proof, so verify promises about health or study results before acting.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the best synthesis of their discussion?
questions.context: You hear two classmates discuss whether to present with video or live interviews.

options.text: Video saves time but interviews give fresher answers, so mix both parts
options.feedback: Correct! Video saves time but interviews give fresher answers, so mix both parts combines both views because one values efficiency and the other values direct voices.

options.text: Video and interviews are both useless and should be banned
options.feedback: The option about both are useless and should be banned is wrong because neither speaker rejects both formats, so it invents a negative agreement they never reach.

options.text: Only video matters because classmates never tell the truth
options.feedback: The option about only video matters because classmates lie is wrong because it keeps one side and insults classmates, ignoring the value of live answers discussed.

options.text: Only interviews matter because video equipment always fails
options.feedback: The option about only interviews matter because equipment fails is wrong because it keeps the other side only and turns a time concern into a false technical failure.

questions.explanation: Synthesizing a discussion means holding both speakers positions together and finding the compromise they point toward. Note each preference plus its reason, then choose the option that honors both reasons.
questions.subject: ingles
